title: Two Brothers, One Birthright
overview: Abraham dies and his family lines are traced, then Isaac's twin sons Esau and Jacob are born already at odds, and Esau trades away his rights as firstborn for a meal.

parts.label: Abraham's other sons (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Keturah was a later wife, and several names in her line, like her son Midian and her grandsons Sheba and Dedan through Jokshan, match peoples of Arabia known later in the Bible. Abraham made Isaac his main heir but gave the other sons gifts while he was alive and sent them east, so no one could dispute the inheritance.

parts.label: Abraham dies and is buried (vv. 7-11)
parts.note: "Gathered to his people" is an old way of saying he died and joined his ancestors. Isaac and Ishmael, long separated, bury him together in the cave he had bought for Sarah, the only land he ever owned in Canaan.

parts.label: Ishmael's family line (vv. 12-18)
parts.note: Ishmael's twelve sons become leaders of tribes in the northern Arabian desert, matching the earlier promise that he too would become a great nation. The last line is hard to translate: it may mean his people lived in conflict with their relatives, or simply that they settled alongside them.

parts.label: Twins in conflict (vv. 19-26)
parts.note: After twenty years without children, Rebekah conceives twins, and the LORD explains their struggling in the womb as two future nations, Israel from Jacob and Edom from Esau, with the younger coming out on top. The names are wordplay: Esau's hairiness echoes Seir, Edom's later homeland, and Jacob sounds like the Hebrew for "heel," hinting at someone who grabs at others or trips them up.

parts.label: The birthright sold (vv. 27-34)
parts.note: Each parent has a favorite son, which sets up trouble later. The birthright meant the eldest son's larger share of the inheritance and leadership of the family, and the story faults Esau for trading it for stew, while Jacob's hard bargain is told without any praise.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether "the older will serve the younger," which the apostle Paul later quotes, is mainly about God choosing individuals for salvation or about the roles of two nations in history.
think: When have you seen someone, maybe yourself, give up something of lasting value for what felt urgent in the moment, and how did it look afterward?
